The article misses out why Kenta / taki (east and west Japan calls it different ... Only old people say kentakki ) actually was able to do this.

Japan after the war was really poor. So, new year's was always given a priority since that is when city dwellers head home to parents out in the country side. Christmas and birthdays really didn't pick up until Japan started on massive exports.

Since New Year's is a splurge on food which are normally traditional dishes (recently more modern items slip in on day 2 and 3), many Japanese did sort of celebrate Christmas. Many areas that had contact with American Soldiers would have cake for Christmas. Cake wasn't cheap so it was special. This evolved slowly into a national event and giving gifts to children eventually caught on to fair number of families. However, the gift is left by the child's pillow so when they woke up they'd be surprised.

Giving gifts to family members hasn't really caught on and many older people just do the gift to grandkids only.

In the mid 80's with a massive disposable income at hand couples turned Christmas in a very "holy" night. They'd go out to dinner, exchange gifts and then head to a live hotel or if funds where available to a hotel -- think prom for every year you're not married :-D

This generation is now in their 40-50's but they still don't really give gifts to each other and fall back to kids only. Older kids normally pocket about $50 cash whole younger ones get toys.
